description: Width tiers for Science Year 1–2 band — ACARA v9. Covers H-strand (Science as a Human Endeavour) and I-strand (Science Inquiry) for the 1–2 year band. U-strand descriptors are in science_y1_width_tiers.json and science_y2_width_tiers.json.
subject: Science

width_notes.minimum_width: For H-strand: science-in-daily-life and pattern-prediction met in one case each. For I-strand: the skill applied in one guided investigation context.
width_notes.typical_width: Full scope across the range of task contexts typical for the 1–2 band, with appropriate teacher guidance.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment adding phenomena, cultural contexts or task types. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations treated as source data.

AC9S1H01.minimum_width: Describe two examples of people using science knowledge in daily life; describe one pattern in nature and one prediction people make based on that pattern.
AC9S1H01.typical_width: Describe multiple examples of science use in daily life across different contexts (farming, wildlife care, engineering, weather forecasting); explain the science knowledge behind each example; describe how observed patterns in weather, seasons and animal behaviour guide predictions and decisions.
wider: Learn from farmers, bush care volunteers, gardeners or nursery owners about how they observe plant and animal needs
Investigate how First Nations Australians use science to meet needs including food, water supply and shelter
Recognise how First Nations Australians use changes in landscape and sky to know when to gather certain resources
Explore how engineers use knowledge of forces to create playground equipment or toys
elaborations: learning from farmers, bush care volunteers, gardeners or nursery owners about observing plant needs
identifying ways science knowledge is used in care of the local environment
investigating how First Nations Australians use science to meet needs including food, water and shelter
recognising how First Nations Australians use landscape and sky changes to answer questions about resource gathering
learning from ecologists or wildlife carers about observing animal behaviour
sharing examples of using science knowledge at home — weather forecasts, seasonal clothing
identifying pushes and pulls when preparing meals and tools that help
exploring how engineers use force knowledge to create playground equipment or toys

AC9S2H01.minimum_width: Describe two examples of people using science knowledge in daily life; describe one sky pattern and one prediction astronomers or First Nations Australians make based on it.
AC9S2H01.typical_width: Describe how astronomers use celestial body patterns to make predictions; describe how musicians understand music as sound patterns; describe how people use voice patterns in technology; examine how material workers use science knowledge; describe how First Nations Australians use science practices including sorting and prediction.
wider: Learn how First Nations Australians use observations of the night sky to assist with navigation
Recognise that astronomers use movement patterns of celestial bodies to predict future appearances
Learn from musicians about how music can be understood as patterns of sounds
Explore how sound-activated and voice-activated tools help people manage daily activities
Learn from material workers (woodworkers, fibre artists) about learning material properties and using creativity
elaborations: learning how First Nations Australians use night sky observations for navigation
recognising that astronomers use celestial body patterns to make predictions
listening to music and learning how musicians use patterns of sounds
discussing how we manage sound at home
investigating voice-activated tools and how they use voice patterns
exploring how sound-activated tools help manage daily activities
learning from material workers about properties and creativity
exploring how physically changing materials decreases waste
considering how First Nations Australians use sorting, classification and estimation to make predictions

AC9S1I01.minimum_width: Pose one question about a pattern or relationship for a given observation; make one prediction and explain what experience it is based on.
AC9S1I01.typical_width: Pose questions about patterns and relationships across Y1 science contexts (habitat needs, force effects, seasonal changes); make experience-based predictions; explain what each question is trying to find out and what experience grounds each prediction.
wider: Pose questions about push-pull relationships: 'Does a toy car go further if pushed harder?'
Make predictions about patterns of seasonal plant changes or temperature across seasons
Make predictions about types of animals they might observe in a particular place
elaborations: posing questions about push and pull relationships
posing questions about how animals meet their needs in particular places
making predictions about plant needs
making predictions about animals and plants in a particular place
making predictions about patterns of seasonal changes or temperature

AC9S2I01.minimum_width: Pose one question about a pattern or relationship in a Y2 science context; make one prediction and explain what experience grounds it.
AC9S2I01.typical_width: Pose questions about patterns in Y2 science contexts (sound properties, sky patterns, material changes); make predictions about future sky appearances, sound-vibration relationships, and material change outcomes; explain the observational basis for each prediction.
wider: Pose questions about how to make sounds with different instruments: 'If I do this, will it produce a higher pitch?'
Make predictions about future moon appearances at certain times of week or month
Make predictions about sound and vibration: 'I think a harder twang will make a louder sound'
elaborations: posing questions about making sounds with different instruments
posing questions about celestial object appearance across time
making predictions about material changes when pulled with different strengths
making predictions about vibration and sound relationships
making predictions about future sky phenomena

AC9S1I02.typical_width: Suggest safety measures across investigation types; follow guided investigation steps; suggest ways to make investigations safer; contribute to equipment set up and pack away.
wider: Explore different ways of investigating science questions through guided discussion

AC9S2I02.minimum_width: Suggest one safety measure for a Y2 investigation and follow visual or verbal steps to conduct it.
AC9S2I02.typical_width: Show appropriate use of materials and equipment; suggest ways to make investigations safer; follow visual or verbal steps to construct an instrument or manipulate a material; discuss safe sun observation methods.
wider: Show appropriate equipment use to others and make suggestions about making an investigation safe
Discuss ways to observe the sun safely

AC9S1I03.minimum_width: Make and record observations in at least two formats (drawing and informal measurement) for a given investigation; explain what an observation is.
AC9S1I03.typical_width: Make observations using senses and tools; use informal measurements (cups, handspans, paces, blocks, string); record observations through text, drawing, counts, digital photography; explain what an observation is.
wider: Use informal measurements to quantify plant growth and object movement
Compare digital photography with hand-drawn recording for the same observation

AC9S2I03.typical_width: Record observations through text, drawing, counts, digital photography or video; use familiar informal units; use digital tools (clap-o-meter apps, time-lapse photography, slow-motion video); engage in guided discussion about fair measurement.
wider: Use chalk lines and string lengths to measure shadows — connecting informal measurement to concrete representation
Explore how simple clap-o-meter apps measure sound volume — examining digital measurement tools
Use time-lapse photography for celestial object movement or slow-motion video for vibrating ruler

representing informal measurements with concrete objects such as chalk lines and string
